connection: Session 06 created a fully initialized Employee and an open ClockEntry with required EmployeeId and ClockIn values. Session 07 first evaluates that existing property design, then extends only ClockEntry with nullable clock-out state and completion invariants.
objectives: Classify each model property as required, legitimately nullable, or meaningfully defaulted.
Explain why Employee needs no initialization change when its constructor assigns every required property.
Explain how a private setter plus a nullable type together model "not yet clocked out".
Protect ClockEntry completion and duration with guard clauses.

visuals.title: Nullable means value or no value
visuals.explanation: DateTime? ClockOut explicitly permits either a real clock-out timestamp or null; every reader of ClockOut must account for both.

visuals.title: Construction guards required state
visuals.explanation: ClockEntry assigns EmployeeId and ClockIn in the constructor, so every successfully created object satisfies those requirements immediately.

visuals.title: The constructor already proves required state
visuals.explanation: Employee's constructor requires and assigns EmployeeId, Name, and Address. Do not add nullable markers or invented defaults when the existing construction path already proves valid initialization.

visuals.title: A null check proves the completed path
visuals.explanation: GetDuration rejects an open entry. After that guard, the method can safely use ClockOut.Value to calculate the completed duration.

preQuiz.prompt: Which ClockEntry value is genuinely optional while an employee is still working?
preQuiz.explanation: An open entry has no clock-out time yet.

preQuiz.prompt: Where should the rule preventing a second clock-out live?
preQuiz.explanation: The model owns the state transition.

preQuiz.prompt: What does a null check give the compiler?
options: Proof for the checked control-flow path
preQuiz.explanation: Nullable flow analysis follows explicit checks.

concept.title: Required state belongs in construction
paragraphs: EmployeeId, Name, and Address are required from the moment an Employee exists. Session 06's constructor receives and assigns all three, so Employee is already fully initialized and does not need a Session 07 code change.
Do not add ? or an empty default merely to silence the compiler. Use nullable only when absence is a valid domain state, and use a default only when that default has real business meaning.

rows: A valid Employee needs a name
A valid Employee needs an address
An open ClockEntry has no clock-out time yet

concept.title: Flow analysis follows the null check
paragraphs: Before clock-out, ClockOut is null. After a guard proves it has a value, the completed path can safely use ClockOut.Value.
The compiler tracks that proof through the local control flow; it does not guess business intent.

concept.title: Invariants reject impossible transitions
paragraphs: Clock-out cannot precede clock-in, and a completed entry cannot be completed again. Those are ClockEntry rules, so ClockEntry protects them.
Callers do not need to remember a fragile sequence of property assignments.

commit: session-06: teach initialization nullability and invariants
review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Employee remains unchanged because its constructor already initializes every required property.
ClockOut is nullable because an open entry legitimately has no clock-out time.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

options: Because an open entry has not completed
postQuiz.explanation: Null represents a real open state.

postQuiz.prompt: What should GetDuration do for an open entry?
postQuiz.explanation: An open entry has no completed duration.

options: So completion passes through the invariant-protecting method
Because nullable properties must be private

reflections: Which ClockEntry values are required versus only-sometimes-present, and why?
Why does Employee need no code change when its constructor already assigns EmployeeId, Name, and Address?
Why would an empty-string default hide rather than solve a missing required value?
whatBreaks: Making ClockOut's setter public lets any code close an entry without going through ClockOutEmployee, bypassing the completion guards. Removing the second-completion or time-order guard permits impossible transitions. Removing the open-entry check from GetDuration makes the method use a clock-out value that does not yet exist.
summary: Employee's constructor already guarantees its required non-null state, so Session 07 leaves it unchanged. ClockEntry.ClockOut uses DateTime? because absence is valid while an entry is open, and its private setter plus guard methods protect valid completion and duration behavior.
